| [LIT-035](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-035.md) v2 | The ergodicity solution of the cooperation puzzle | Peters & Adamou (2022), DOI-10.1098/rsta.2020.0425. The premium is (σ²/2)(1 − 1/N) (Eq. 4.2). The proof applies the Eilenberg–Montgomery/Begle fixed-point theorem to the product best-response map. | [LIT-282](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-282.md) v2 | The Possibility of Social Choice | Sen (1998), DOI-10.1257/aer.89.3.349. Sen argues that utilitarian equality (equal marginal utility), total-utility equality (completed as leximin) and Rawlsian equality (maximin/leximin on an index of primary goods) are each insufficient, and so is any combination of them, even for the needs-based part of equality: the test case is a disabled person who has no marginal-utility claim, no total-utility deprivation (he is contented) and no primary-goods deprivation, yet has an evident claim. He proposes "basic capability equality" — equality in "a person being able to do certain basic things" (p. 218) — as a non-fetishist, culture-dependent extension of Rawls, explicitly only "a partial guide" to the equality part of morality, and says his main (negative) thesis does not depend on this constructive proposal (p. 220). | Active — read in full 2026-09-28 ([NOTE-258](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-258.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of the capability idea and the cleanest short case against welfarist and primary-goods metrics; read it knowing that the positive proposal is a two-page sketch with no account of which capabilities count or how to index them, and that "functionings", "capability sets" and "freedom" do not yet appear. |
| [LIT-379](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-379.md) | Anger makes fake news viral online | Chuai & Zhao (2020), arXiv:2004.10399. On Weibo, fake news carries more anger and less joy than real news, and in observational regressions with controls anger raises retweets while joy lowers them; questionnaires tie anger-dominated news to anxiety-management and information-sharing motives. Unread closely: registered from a triage reading. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-01 from the reading feed, where it was read on three separate days (the anthology's issue 180, https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/180); read for triage, not yet closely enough to place, and no NOTE is filed |
| [LIT-391](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-391.md) v3 | Group Agency: The Possibility, Design, and Status of Corporate Agents | List & Pettit (2011), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199591565.001.0001. Per its publisher, the book argues that "there really are group or corporate agents, over and above the individual agents who compose them", and that social science, law, morality and politics must take account of this. The account is said to be "entirely unmysterious" and grounded in social choice theory, economics and philosophy. Three parts: the logical possibility of group agents (conditions of agency, aggregation of attitudes, structure), their organisational design (epistemic, incentive-compatibility and control desiderata), and their normative status (responsibility, personhood, identification). Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (Oxford Academic is paywalled, and neither author has posted the book or draft chapters), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the book-length case that organised groups are agents over and above their members, which is the composition side's premise in the Minsky–Schwitzgebel bridge; whether it says anything about group consciousness is unknown from what was seen. Rechecked 2026-10-04 with no lawful copy found; two shorter papers by the authors stating Part I's supervenience thesis were read and filed instead ([LIT-705](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-705.md), [LIT-700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-700.md)), and the book stays Deferred because a paper is not a reading of it. |
| [LIT-401](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-401.md) | What is it like to be a group agent? | List (2016), DOI-10.1111/nous.12162. Group agents (firms, courts, states) are real agents in a thin functionalist sense, and they can have consciousness as awareness. Whether they have phenomenal consciousness depends on which psycho-physical bridge principle is true. Under IIT, List argues informally that a group agent's Φ is low: groups decompose into self-contained units, their steering bodies keep working when partly randomised, and most of their processing happens inside individuals. The exclusion postulate would deny group consciousness even if group Φ were high. So group agents are (close to) not conscious, which List uses to ground a normative asymmetry: groups have only derivative rights. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-340](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-340.md)); the standard reply to [LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md) from the group-agency side: it grants that organised groups are agents with functional awareness and argues, conditionally on IIT, that they have little or no phenomenal consciousness. Worth reading for its separation of agency from experience and for its three reasons why a group agent's Φ should be low. The low-Φ verdict is argued informally, with no Φ computed for any group, and the paper never answers the reply Schwitzgebel had already made to the objection its third reason restates. |
| [LIT-424](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-424.md) | From Bacteria to Bach and Back: The Evolution of Minds | Dennett (2017), W. W. Norton. Per its publisher, the book shows "step by step, how a comprehending mind could in fact have arisen from a mindless process of natural selection", with the decisive shift the sharing of memes, which produced "thinking tools" powerful enough that minds "create and comprehend". Its contents run from the origin of reasons and "two strange inversions of reasoning", through information, "brains made of brains", words, memes and the origins of language, to consciousness as "an evolved user-illusion" and "the age of post-intelligent design". Unread: registered from the description and the catalogue's contents note. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the catalogue record's contents note, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive scan is lending-only, Norton posts no excerpt beyond its description, and Dennett posted no draft chapters that I could find. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. The claim the record wants from it, competence without comprehension, is not stated in the description or the contents, so nothing here places it. |
| [LIT-426](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-426.md) | Macrocognition: A Theory of Distributed Minds and Collective Intentionality | Huebner (2014), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199926275.001.0001. Per its publisher, the book argues that genuine cognition requires flexible goal-directed behaviour, which requires specialised representational systems integrated so as to cope fluidly with the environment, and so that collective mentality "should be posited where and only where specialized subroutines are integrated to yield goal-directed behavior that is sensitive to the concerns that are relevant to a group as such". On this view there are many kinds of collective minds, some more like honeybees or cats than people, and groups are unlikely to be full "believers". Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (Oxford Academic is paywalled, the Internet Archive copy is lending-only, and no author-posted draft was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. Of the four works filed for the Minsky–Schwitzgebel bridge it is the one whose criterion for a collective mind is itself a decomposition criterion: mentality wherever specialised subroutines are integrated into goal-directed behaviour sensitive to the group's concerns. A close reading is the most likely of the four to change the bridge. |
| [LIT-472](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-472.md) | Understanding Institutions: The Science and Philosophy of Living Together | Guala (2016), DOI-10.1515/9781400880911. Per its publisher, a unified theory of institutions combining three views (equilibria of strategic games, regulative rules, constitutive rules), applied to money, private property and marriage. It then addresses reflexivity, realism, Verstehen and fallibilism in the social sciences, criticises Hacking's looping effects and interactive kinds, and asks whether causal and ontological dependence can demarcate social from natural science. Only the sample chapter 1 was read: it restates Hindriks & Guala's case against a rules-only account. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description, table of contents, sample chapter and index, not read: the book is not lawfully readable in full online (De Gruyter and Princeton are paywalled, and the Internet Archive has no copy). Only chapter 1, Rules, the publisher's free sample, was read; it is a lightly expanded version of the first section of Hindriks & Guala ([LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md)). It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-473](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-473.md) | Convention: A Philosophical Study | Lewis (1969), DOI-10.1002/9780470693711 (the 2002 Blackwell reissue). The founding analysis of convention as a self-perpetuating solution to a recurring coordination problem with more than one equilibrium, sustained by a system of mutual expectations rather than by agreement, with conventions of language and communication as the main application. Unread: filed from catalogue records and chapter titles; the content summary is as Hindriks & Guala and the SEP entry state it. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from catalogue records and the chapter list, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The Harvard 1969 edition is lending-only at the Internet Archive (access-restricted, printdisabled), and the Wiley-Blackwell reissue of 2002 is paywalled. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |

A treatise in the sociology of knowledge. By its contents: the reality of everyday life and its language; society as objective reality (institutionalization, sedimentation and tradition, roles, legitimation, symbolic universes); society as subjective reality (primary and secondary socialization, identity). Unread: filed from catalogue records and the table of contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records and the 1966 edition's table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scans of the 1966 Doubleday edition and a 1967 printing are lending-only, and there is no author-posted text), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the sociology-of-knowledge treatise whose title phrase [ADR-017](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md)'s topic blurb uses; what it claims, beyond its contents page, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-476](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-476.md) | We-Intentions | Tuomela & Miller (1988), DOI-10.1007/BF00353512, Philosophical Studies 53(3): 367–389. The paper introduces the we-intention: roughly, a group member's intention to do her part of a joint action, together with beliefs that the conditions for the joint action obtain and that this is mutually believed. The concept is applied to simple social practical reasoning and offered as basic to social theory. Unread: filed from metadata, with the content as search summaries report it. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's metadata and reference list; no lawful full text was reachable (Springer is paywalled, the University of Helsinki portal holds only the citation, and the 2020 De Gruyter reprint is closed), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the founding paper of Tuomela's we-intention account, the main analysis Searle's 1990 paper ([LIT-490](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-490.md)) is reported to argue against. |
| [LIT-478](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-478.md) | The Ant Trap: Rebuilding the Foundations of the Social Sciences | Epstein (2015), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199381104.001.0001. Social science works with an "anthropocentric" picture on which the social world is built out of people, as an ant colony is built out of ants. Part One separates the facts that ground a social fact from the facts that anchor the frame principle saying how such facts are grounded, and argues ontological individualism false. Part Two argues that even facts about groups, including group action and intention, are grounded in more than the members. Unread: filed from the introduction, the author's précis and the publisher's description. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the author's own posted introduction and table of contents, not read: the book is not lawfully readable in full online (Oxford Academic is paywalled; the author posts only the introduction). The introduction and the author's open-access précis were read. Its framework, grounding versus anchoring, is stated in the record from the précis and from the author's SEP entry ([LIT-487](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-487.md), read). Part Two argues that facts about groups, including their actions and intentions, are grounded in more than their members, which bears directly on [THEORY-043](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-043.md). It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md) | Institutions, rules, and equilibria: a unified theory | Hindriks & Guala (2015, online 2014), DOI-10.1017/S1744137414000496. Institutions are rules in equilibrium: correlated equilibria of coordination games with several equilibria, which the players represent to themselves as rules. Searle's constitutive rules ("X counts as Y in C") are obtained from a regulative rule by splitting it with a new term, a base rule (X is Y) and a status rule (if Y then Z). The new term is conservative and eliminable, so the constitutive-rules account reduces to the rules-in-equilibrium account, and Lewis's theory of theoretical terms says the term refers if the rules are true. Shown on one toy institution (first-occupancy property); general reduction asserted. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-395](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-395.md)), with the authors' reply to their six commentators in the same issue; worth reading as the shortest statement of the rules-in-equilibrium theory of institutions and of the claim that Searle's constitutive rules are regulative rules with a name added. The equilibrium half is a clear synthesis of Lewis, Aumann, Aoki and Greif. The reduction of constitutive rules is shown on one toy institution and asserted in general, and it leans on a reading of "collective acceptance" loose enough to make it hard to fail. |
| [LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md) | Social ontology: Some basic principles | Searle (2006), DOI-10.1177/1463499606061731. Institutional reality is built from three primitives: collective intentionality, the assignment of function, and constitutive rules of the form "X counts as Y in C". The Y status is held only by collective acceptance, and it carries deontic powers, which are desire-independent reasons for action. Institutional facts need language because they exist only as represented. Two revisions of the 1995 book: status indicators (after De Soto), and "free-standing Y terms" (after Barry Smith), such as corporations and money without currency. In those cases there is no X, and "We accept (S has power (S does A))", a formula from later in the book, is ranked as the more general form. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-388](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-388.md)), in its parallel English printing in Papers: Revista de Sociologia 80 (2006), pp. 51–71, not in the Anthropological Theory typesetting the DOI names; worth reading as Searle's own short restatement of The Construction of Social Reality ([LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md)), and as the place where he concedes that "X counts as Y in C" is not the general form. Status functions imposed by collective acceptance carry deontic powers, and deontic powers are desire-independent reasons for action. Read it for the structure, not for an argument about collective intentionality: that is taken as a primitive and referred to his 1990 paper ([LIT-490](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-490.md)), not defended here. |
| [LIT-484](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-484.md) | Qu'est-ce qu'un fait social ? | Durkheim (1894; book 1895), ch. I of Les Règles de la méthode sociologique. A social fact is "toute manière de faire, fixée ou non, susceptible d'exercer sur l'individu une contrainte extérieure", or equivalently one general in a society while existing independently of its individual manifestations. Such facts are neither organic nor individual-psychic, so their substrate is society. They are general because collective, not collective because general: "il est dans chaque partie parce qu'il est dans le tout". Ways of being (morphology) are consolidated ways of doing. A definition argued from examples, not proved. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-391](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-391.md)); worth reading as the founding definition of a social fact, and as a short text later social ontology still cites (Ritchie 2018 does, for the group as more than a sum). Fifteen pages define the object of sociology by two marks, exteriority to individual consciousness and external constraint, with diffusion plus independent existence as an equivalent second test. It is a definition, not an argument: Durkheim calls it "un simple résumé des données immédiates de lobservation" (n. 3), and its two load-bearing steps (that what is neither organic nor individual-psychic must have society as its substrate, and that constraint is present even where nobody feels it) are asserted from examples. Read for the vocabulary and the part-whole thesis ("il est dans chaque partie parce qu'il est dans le tout"), not for a proof. |
| [LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md) | The Construction of Social Reality | Searle (1995), Free Press, New York (xiii + 241 pp.). The founding book of Searle's social ontology. Per its catalogue description, it argues that some facts are independent of human observers and some require human agreement. Its chapters move from the building blocks of social reality and the creation of institutional facts through language and a general theory of institutional facts, to a defence of external realism and the correspondence theory of truth. Unread: filed from the catalogue record and contents; the record reads the theory in Searle's 2006 restatement. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from catalogue records and a library scan of the table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in print with Free Press / Simon & Schuster, the Internet Archive copies are either lending-only or unauthorised uploads, and Searle posted no draft), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. The record reads the theory through Searle's own 2006 restatement ([LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md), read in full), which is the entry to start from. |
| [LIT-487](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-487.md) | Social Ontology | Epstein (2018; rev. 2024), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/social-ontology/>. A survey that splits social ontology into two inquiries: what determines (grounds) a social fact, and what constructs or "anchors" the category it falls under, likened to semantics and metasemantics. §3 surveys determination bases (psychologism, atomism, bodies and practices, physicalism, holism, flat ontologies) and reports that ontological individualism is widely assumed and recently contested. §4 surveys anchoring theories (agreement, Lewis's convention, Hart and Searle's collective acceptance, patterns, practices, language). §5 covers groups, group minds and agency, institutions, race and gender, artifacts, money, law and language. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-393](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-393.md)); worth reading as a survey: the best single map of social ontology in the record, organised around its author's distinction between what grounds a social fact (§3) and what anchors, or sets up, the category it falls under (§4). It is also the record's readable source for what The Ant Trap's grounding–anchoring framework is ([LIT-478](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-478.md) is not lawfully readable). Read it as a survey written by a partisan: Epstein's own positions organise the entry, and the critics of anchoring are named but given a sentence each. |
| [LIT-489](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-489.md) | Institutions | North (1991), DOI-10.1257/jep.5.1.97. Institutions are "the humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and social interaction": informal constraints (taboos, customs, codes of conduct) and formal rules (constitutions, laws, property rights). With technology they set transaction and production costs, and so the incentive structure of an economy. Tribal exchange, the Suq and the caravan trade did not evolve from within; early modern European trade did, through merchant law, bills of exchange, insurance and a state bound not to confiscate. Institutional change is path dependent because the institutional matrix has increasing returns. A narrative essay; the definition is stipulated. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-392](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-392.md)); worth reading as the economist's canonical one-paragraph definition of institutions ("the humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and social interaction") and as a compact statement of the transaction-cost and path-dependence programme. It is an essay, not an argument: the game-theoretic motivation is one paragraph, the history is narrative, and the definition is stipulated, not defended. For what an institution is, read it beside Hindriks & Guala ([LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md)), who take it as the exemplar of the rules account and say what it leaves out. |
| [LIT-492](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-492.md) | On Social Facts | Gilbert (1989), Routledge (reissued by Princeton University Press, 1992; DOI-10.1515/9780691214627). The book asks whether social groups are real over and above individuals' thoughts. It analyses everyday concepts of social action, social groups, collective belief and social convention, in dialogue with Weber, Simmel, Durkheim and David Lewis, and proposes that core social phenomena are "plural subject" phenomena. Unread: filed from the publishers' descriptions and the chapter list. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publishers' records and the chapter list; no lawful full text was reachable (the Princeton reissue is sold as an e-book on De Gruyter, and the Internet Archive's copy of the Routledge edition is lending-only), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is Gilbert's book-length treatment of plural subjects, collective belief and social convention; "Walking Together" ([LIT-477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-477.md)) is the short version. |
| [LIT-493](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-493.md) | The Grammar of Society: The Nature and Dynamics of Social Norms | Bicchieri (2006; print December 2005), DOI-10.1017/CBO9780511616037. Per its publisher, an integrated account, drawing on social psychology, experimental economics and evolutionary game theory, of how social norms such as fairness, cooperation and reciprocity emerge, why and when people follow them, when they attend to the relevant norm, why inefficient norms survive, and how psychological dispositions can lead to fairness norms like ours. Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. Cambridge Core is paywalled. The author's own copy of chapter 1 on her University of Pennsylvania pages and the publisher's excerpt at assets.cambridge.org both failed (HTTP 403; connection reset), and the Internet Archive has no copy. It is the standard equilibrium-and-expectations account of social norms; what its definition of a norm says was not seen. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |

By the publisher's account, moral questions arise from conflicts of interest, and moral systems use confluences of interest at lower levels of organization to manage conflicts at higher ones; they are "systems of indirect reciprocity", run on reputation, and morality arose within groups for unity in intergroup competition. Unread: filed from the publisher's description and chapter titles. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The 1987 Aldine de Gruyter edition is lending-only at the Internet Archive (access-restricted, printdisabled), and the 2017 Routledge reissue is paywalled. | [LIT-496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-496.md) | Mapping morality with a compass: Testing the theory of ‘morality-as-cooperation’ with a new questionnaire | Curry, Jones Chesters & Van Lissa (2019), DOI-10.1016/j.jrp.2018.10.008. The Morality-as-Cooperation Questionnaire, 21 Relevance and 21 Judgement items for seven domains, tested in UK (n = 1,392) and US (n = 469) online samples against the MFQ (UK n = 1,042). Seven factors fit the Relevance items (CFI .98) but not the Judgement items (CFI .87), and the combined seven-domain model is rejected (CFI .73). The MFQ's five factors fit worse. MFQ purity items are rated about as morally relevant as its loyalty and authority items, which the authors concede contradicts the theory. | Proposed — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-412](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-412.md)), from the PsyArXiv manuscript; worth reading as the programme's psychometric test and as the place its authors concede that purity items are rated morally relevant, which "appear[s] to contradict" the theory. Its seven-factor result is weaker than the abstract says. The items were written by the authors, three per domain, from the theory itself, and selected by fit within each domain. Seven factors then fit the Relevance items but not the Judgement items, and the combined seven-domain model is rejected (CFI .73), so the best model has fourteen correlated factors. No non-cooperative item is in the MAC-Q, so it cannot test whether morality is only about cooperation. It would be settled by an item pool written independently of the theory, with harm, purity and other non-cooperative content in it, factored blind, on data that can be shared. |
| [LIT-499](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-499.md) | Moral Foundations Theory: The Pragmatic Validity of Moral Pluralism | Graham et al. (2013), DOI-10.1016/B978-0-12-407236-7.00002-4. Moral Foundations Theory in full: a nativist, cultural-developmental, intuitionist and pluralist account with five foundations (Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority, Sanctity), each tied to an adaptive challenge and an existing evolutionary model. A decade of MFQ work finds liberals rely on Care and Fairness, conservatives on all five, across 12 world regions. Five criteria for "foundationhood" are proposed, and Liberty, Efficiency, Ownership and Honesty are named candidates. Harm monism (Gray) and fairness monism (Baumard) are rejected as Procrustean. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-396](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-396.md)); worth reading as the full statement of Moral Foundations Theory and as the text to check morality-as-cooperation's comparison against. It states the theory's four claims (nativism, cultural learning, intuitionism, pluralism), reviews a decade of MFQ findings, mostly on political ideology, and offers five criteria for what counts as a foundation. By its own table the Care foundation rests on kin selection and Fairness on Trivers' reciprocal altruism, and Ownership/theft is already a named candidate, so the claim that MFT omits kin altruism, reciprocal altruism and property does not survive this text. Sanctity, the foundation morality-as-cooperation excludes, is by the same table the one with the least evidence of innate preparedness. |
| [LIT-500](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-500.md) | Morality beyond the WEIRD: How the nomological network of morality varies across cultures | Atari et al. (2023), DOI-10.1037/pspp0000470. The Moral Foundations Questionnaire-2: 36 items, six per foundation, for Care, Equality, Proportionality, Loyalty, Authority and Purity, built and tested on 25 populations (N ≈ 8,700) in local languages. Equality and Proportionality correlate weakly (mean r = .21). Purity is the foundation most related to cultural distance from the U.S. (r = .43) and to religiosity. The individualizing–binding split appears in only three of 19 national networks. The MFQ-2 explains more variance in 30 criterion scores than the MFQ-1 (mean adjusted R² .37 against .30). | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-398](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-398.md)), from the APA accepted manuscript; worth reading as the current Moral Foundations measure (the MFQ-2) and the theory's current list of six foundations, with Fairness split into Equality and Proportionality, and as the place MFT answers morality-as-cooperation directly: Curry et al. 2019 "left out Purity as an important and less-WEIRD moral foundation". Its strongest evidence for that, Purity's association with cultural distance from the U.S., rests on the one subscale that fails its own measurement-invariance threshold. Its samples are online panels in 25 populations, not small-scale societies. |
| [LIT-502](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-502.md) | Intuitive ethics: how innately prepared intuitions generate culturally variable virtues | Haidt & Joseph (2004), DOI-10.1162/0011526042365555. Proposes that people are innately prepared to feel flashes of approval or disapproval at four patterns: suffering, hierarchy, reciprocity and purity, with ingroup the best candidate for a fifth (fn. 15). Each is a module with a proper domain it evolved for (one's own child in distress; cheating in joint ventures; disease and waste) and a culturally widened actual domain. Cultures build virtues on these intuitions and differ in which they use. The four were chosen by counting which concerns appeared in five surveyed works; the essay reports no data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-400](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-400.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of Moral Foundations Theory, and as the text morality-as-cooperation quotes when it calls purity non-cooperative. It proposes four innately prepared intuition "modules" (suffering, hierarchy, reciprocity, purity), with ingroup as a likely fifth in a footnote, and argues that cultures build virtues on them. The list comes from tallying five books, not from data, and no study is reported. It already grounds the suffering module in care for one's own children and the reciprocity module in Trivers, so the later charge that the foundations omit kin and reciprocal altruism does not fit this text. |
| [LIT-503](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-503.md) | Morality as Cooperation: A Problem-Centred Approach | Curry (2016), DOI-10.1007/978-3-319-19671-8_2. Morality is "a collection of biological and cultural solutions to the problems of cooperation and conflict recurrent in human social life". Nonzero-sum game theory yields seven problems (kin, coordination, exchange, hawkish and dovish contest displays, division, possession) and hence seven moral domains, illustrated but not tested. The chapter predicts that non-cooperative behaviour is morally neutral everywhere, and that MFT's purity domain has no connection to cooperation. | Proposed — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-408](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-408.md)); the founding statement of morality-as-cooperation and the place its predictions are stated most sharply, including the one its own tests have not run: that behaviour unrelated to cooperation will be morally neutral, and that no culture's morality will be about "aesthetics or nutrition" (p. 40). It reports no data. The seven domains are derived from game theory and then illustrated with quotations from philosophers and ethnographers, so the chapter shows the taxonomy is coherent, not that it is the right one. It would be settled by the test [LIT-047](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-047.md) lacks: blind coding of all moralized content in one sample, asking whether non-cooperative domains are moralized. |
| [LIT-504](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-504.md) | A Natural History of Human Morality | Tomasello (2016), DOI-10.4159/9780674915855. By the publisher's account, a reconstruction from experiments comparing great apes and children of how early humans became "an ultra-cooperative and, eventually, a moral species". The chapter titles give the steps: an interdependence hypothesis, a second-personal morality of collaborating partners, an "objective" morality of the cultural group, and human morality as "cooperation-plus". Unread: filed from the description and chapter list. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The book is lending-only at the Internet Archive (access-restricted, printdisabled) and paywalled at Harvard University Press and De Gruyter. Its relation to Tomasello's later "The moral psychology of obligation" ([LIT-125](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-125.md), read in [NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md)) is inferred from the chapter titles and that reading, and is labelled as inference. An author's précis exists (Philosophical Psychology, 2018, DOI 10.1080/09515089.2018.1486605) and was not read; it would be the natural first step. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-507](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-507.md) | Moral psychology is relationship regulation: Moral motives for unity, hierarchy, equality, and proportionality | Rai & Fiske (2011), DOI-10.1037/a0021867. Relationship regulation theory: moral judgments are not about features of acts (harm, unfairness, impurity) but about whether acts fit the relationship model in force. Fiske's four relational models each carry a moral motive: Unity (communal sharing), Hierarchy (authority ranking), Equality (equality matching) and Proportionality (market pricing). The motives are universal; cultures differ in where they apply them. So violence, inequality and "impure" acts can be morally required, and purity and ingroup loyalty are one motive. A review, with no new data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-405](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-405.md)); worth reading as the relational alternative to both Moral Foundations Theory and morality-as-cooperation, and as the source of the Equality/Proportionality split the MFQ-2 later adopted. It is a theoretical review with no new data. It agrees with morality-as-cooperation that morality exists to sustain cooperative relationships, and differs from it on purity (a Unity motive, the same motive as ingroup loyalty), on harm (violence can be morally required) and on the units (four relational models, not seven game-theoretic problems). |
| [LIT-508](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-508.md) | A mutualistic approach to morality: The evolution of fairness by partner choice | Baumard, André & Sperber (2013), DOI-10.1017/S0140525X11002202. When individuals can choose partners and have equal outside options, a split that gives one side less than it could get elsewhere is not stable, so partner choice selects for sharing the gains of cooperation in proportion to contribution. Competition to be chosen then favours a genuine, non-instrumental sense of fairness. Economic-game results (entitlement effects, merit-based division, need-based mutual aid, proportionate punishment) are reinterpreted as fairness, not altruism. Morality is defined as fairness; kin care and group loyalty are not intrinsically moral. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-407](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-407.md)), with all 28 open peer commentaries and the authors' Response; worth reading as the strongest single-mechanism cooperative theory of morality and as the parent of moral disciplining ([LIT-101](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-101.md)). It is a cooperation theory that cuts the other way from morality-as-cooperation: partner choice selects one moral sense, fairness, and kin care and group loyalty are not intrinsically moral. Its evidence is a reinterpretation of others' economic-game results, and its central formal claim is cited from the authors' separate model. The commentaries (Graham, Ramlakhan & Brook, Machery & Stich, Sachdeva et al., Atran) press the purity, harm and scope objections, and the Response answers them two ways because the authors disagree among themselves. |
| [LIT-509](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-509.md) | Moral Molecules: Morality as a Combinatorial System | Curry, Alfano, Brandt & Pelican (2021), DOI-10.1007/s13164-021-00540-x. The seven morality-as-cooperation domains are treated as elements that combine into "molecules". For each of the 21 pairs a moral concept is proposed and an example found in the literature: fraternity, blood revenge, filial piety, honour, queuing and so on. Counting combinations gives 127 positive molecules and 2,186 of mixed valence. The test is confirmatory: no search protocol, blind judges or failed searches are reported. | Proposed — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-399](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-399.md)); a clear statement of the programme's ambition, that seven cooperative elements generate "all moral ideas, possible and actual", but its test is the weakest in the programme. For each of the 21 pairs the authors proposed a concept and then searched the literature until they found it ("We succeeded in every case"). No search protocol, judges or failed attempts are reported, and the theory "doesn't predict which of these many possibilities will be actualities". Two molecules (mendicance, common ownership) combine an element with the negation of another, which the paper's own notation counts as mixed valence. It would be settled by blind judges classifying an independent list of moral concepts into the scheme, with a count of those that fit nothing. |
| [LIT-510](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-510.md) | The Evolution of Reciprocal Altruism | Trivers (1971), DOI-10.1086/406755. Altruism between non-relatives can be selected if acts cost the giver less than they benefit the recipient, the same partners meet repeatedly and symmetrically, and altruists stop helping those who fail to reciprocate. Cleaner-fish hosts fit; bird alarm calls are explained instead by self-interest. In humans, friendship, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, guilt, suspicion and their sham versions are proposed as adaptations that regulate exchange, and rules of conduct as a multiparty extension. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-402](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-402.md)); worth reading as the source of reciprocal altruism and, for this record above all, of the first adaptive account of moral emotions: moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, guilt and the detection of sham versions of each, with "norms of reciprocal conduct" as a later step. The formal part is slight (a verbal model and Hamilton's communicated Prisoner's Dilemma sketch); the human psychology is hypothesis supported by the social-psychology literature of the 1960s. It grounds the exchange domain of morality-as-cooperation and gives that domain its emotions. |
| [LIT-511](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-511.md) | The emotional dog and its rational tail: A social intuitionist approach to moral judgment | Haidt (2001), DOI-10.1037/0033-295X.108.4.814. Moral judgment is usually caused by fast affective intuitions; moral reasoning mostly comes after, to justify the judgment to others, and changes minds chiefly by triggering new intuitions in listeners. Four reasons are offered: two processing systems, motivated reasoning, post-hoc confabulation, and the weak link between moral reasoning and moral action. Intuitions are partly innate and are tuned by culture through custom complexes and peers in late childhood. Harmless taboo violations are condemned anyway, and people are "dumbfounded" when their reasons run out. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-403](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-403.md)), from the author's final manuscript; worth reading as the standard statement of the social intuitionist model, the proximate account of moral judgment that morality-as-cooperation lacks, and as the source of the "harmless wrongs" (consensual incest, sex with a dead chicken) on which the purity and sex objections to cooperative theories rest. Most of its evidence comes from outside the moral domain, which the author says himself: the model is offered as "a plausible alternative", not an established fact. |
| [LIT-512](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-512.md) | Moral universals: A machine-reading analysis of 256 societies | Alfano, Cheong & Curry (2024), DOI-10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e25940. A word-count dictionary for the seven morality-as-cooperation domains (MAC-D, built by expert brainstorming and WordNet expansion) is run over 9,653 eHRAF Ethics paragraphs from 256 societies. Most morals are detected in most societies, with small but significant differences by region and subsistence. Against the earlier hand codes the dictionary agrees only slightly to fairly (κ .08–.25) and overstates prevalence. It cannot tell praise from condemnation, so it says nothing about valence. | Proposed — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-406](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-406.md)); worth reading for the Morality-as-Cooperation Dictionary and for what it shows about the sixty-society result, not as a replication of it. The dictionary counts words and, by the authors' own statement, "cannot be used to estimate the moral valence of cooperation", so it does not test the 961-of-962 finding at all. Its agreement with the earlier hand codes is slight to fair (κ .08–.25), and it inflates fairness from 15% to 58% of societies. It detects significant, though small, regional differences, against the earlier claim of equal frequency. A spot-check of its paragraphs found admired theft in four more societies. It would be settled by valence-aware coding validated against blind hand codes, run with dictionaries for non-cooperative domains on the same corpus. |
| [LIT-513](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-513.md) | Validation of Morality as Cooperation Questionnaire in Turkey, and Its Relation to Prosociality, Ideology, and Resource Scarcity | Yilmaz, Harma & Doğruyol (2021), DOI-10.1027/1015-5759/a000627. In Turkish undergraduates (n = 445), the MAC-Q's seven-factor model fits the Relevance items (CFI .949, RMSEA .053) but not the Judgement items or the full form, as in the original. Deference and family track resistance to change, and fairness tracks lower opposition to equality. Resource-scarcity primes in Turkey (n = 576) and a preregistered US study (n = 921) change nothing. Relevance scores correlate modestly with prosocial intentions. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-397](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-397.md)), from the accepted manuscript; worth reading as the first independent test of the MAC-Q, by a team with no morality-as-cooperation author. It reproduces the questionnaire's main result in Turkish undergraduates (n = 445): seven factors fit the Relevance items (CFI .949) and fail on the Judgement items (CFI .828) and the full form (CFI .752). Its two resource-scarcity experiments are null. Its scope is narrow: there is no non-cooperative item, so it tests MAC's structure, not its claim that morality is only cooperation; and the latent correlations (fairness–property .87, family–group .80) and a second-order single factor fitting at CFI .906 limit how distinct the seven are. |
| [LIT-514](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-514.md) | Moral Origins: The Evolution of Virtue, Altruism, and Shame | Boehm (2012), Basic Books. By the publisher's account, the moral sense is "a sophisticated defense mechanism": group punishment of bullies, thieves, free riders and psychopaths over six million years made social selection favour altruists and bred conscience, virtue and shame. The chapter list adds a "selection-by-reputation hypothesis" and its test. Unread: filed from the description and chapter list. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The book is lending-only at the Internet Archive (item moraloriginsevol0000boeh) and sold by Basic Books. What it argues is known here only from the publisher's description, labelled as such. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-538.md) | How effective psychological treatments work: mechanisms of change in cognitive behavioural therapy and beyond | Salkovskis, Sighvatsson & Sigurdsson, Behavioural and Cognitive Psychotherapy 51(6):595–615, in the special issue "Disseminating CBT: 50 years and beyond" (issue dated November 2023, first published online 5 January 2024). A history of behaviour therapy and CBT as empirically grounded treatment development, an argument that common factors are not mechanisms of change, and a proposal: the mechanism of all effective therapies is a shift from a stuck, threat-laden meaning ("Theory A") to a collaboratively built and tested alternative ("Theory B"), which the authors call a type of psychological flexibility. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-428](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-428.md)), from the open-access (CC BY 4.0) publisher PDF; worth reading as a senior Beckian's statement of a single mechanism of change for all effective psychological therapy, and for its clear separation of "common factors" from "mechanisms of change". Its thesis is a proposal argued from the history of CBT and clinical examples, not a tested result: people are "stuck" in an exaggerated negative or threatening meaning (Theory A) kept alive by what it makes them do, and any effective therapy works by helping them build and test a less threatening alternative (Theory B). The paper calls this a particular type of psychological flexibility, without citing the ACT literature that uses that name. |
| [LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md) | Relational Frame Theory: Some Implications for Understanding and Treating Human Psychopathology | Barnes-Holmes, Barnes-Holmes, McHugh & Hayes (2004), International Journal of Psychology and Psychological Therapy 4(2):355–375. RFT stated briefly: humans relate events bidirectionally and arbitrarily, as a generalized operant under contextual control, so words take on the functions of what they are related to. Frames combine into networks, networks are related to networks (metaphor), rules are networks that regulate behaviour, and the self is content, process and context of verbal relations. Psychopathology is read as verbal behaviour, and ACT's acceptance, defusion and values are given RFT interpretations. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-430](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-430.md)), in place of the RFT book, [LIT-549](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-549.md); worth reading as a short statement of Relational Frame Theory by two of the book's editors, and as the paper that shows how RFT is meant to become a theory of psychopathology. Humans, unlike the animals of conditioning research, relate events bidirectionally, so a word acquires the functions of what it names. Relating is a generalized operant learned across exemplars, and its frames share mutual entailment, combinatorial entailment and the transformation of function. Rules are relational networks, and the self is three verbal relations to one's own behaviour. ACT's acceptance, defusion and values are then reinterpreted in those terms. Its clinical examples are illustrations, not data, and it says its Part 3 is "no more than a heuristic". |
| [LIT-543](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-543.md) | Examining Domains of Psychological Flexibility and Inflexibility as Treatment Mechanisms in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: A Comprehensive Systematic and Meta-Analytic Review | Macri & Rogge (2024), Clinical Psychology Review 110:102432. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 77 records (67 studies, N = 9,123). ACT reduced global inflexibility, lack of present-moment awareness, fusion, experiential avoidance, self-as-content and inaction, and increased committed action/values, flexibility/acceptance and defusion, against waitlist and active comparators. Those changes were linked to drops in distress. Unread: registered from the abstract. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the PubMed abstract and Crossref, not read. The article is closed access at Elsevier, it is not in PubMed Central, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy. A web search for a PsyArXiv or OSF preprint found none, and the University of Rochester's repository (UR Research) holds two dissertations from Rogge's lab on the same question (Dubler 2018, Rolffs 2019) but not this review. ScienceDirect itself was not tried. A human reader with Elsevier access could promote this; it is the record's only quantitative test of the ACT process model. |
| [LIT-544](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-544.md) | The Future of Intervention Science: Process-Based Therapy | Hofmann & Hayes (2019; online 2018), Clinical Psychological Science 7(1):37–50. The era of "protocols for syndromes" is over: thirty years of DSM-defined randomised trials never found the diseases the syndromes were meant to reveal. Evidence-based therapy should be redefined as process-based therapy, "evidence-based processes linked to evidence-based procedures", with mediation and moderation as the evidence, functional analysis and idiographic networks as diagnosis, and named therapies and broad schools in decline. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-437](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-437.md)), from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central; worth reading as the programme statement of process-based therapy by the leading figures of the two camps of CBT it reconciles. It replaces "protocols for syndromes" with one question: "What core biopsychosocial processes should be targeted with this client given this goal in this situation, and how can they most efficiently and effectively be changed?" It is a position paper with predictions, not a result. Its sharpest commitment is a falsification rule: an intervention whose specified process of change "cannot be shown to be consistently applicable" has an incorrect model, however well it works. |
| [LIT-545](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-545.md) | Self-Efficacy: Toward a Unifying Theory of Behavioral Change | Bandura (1977), Psychological Review 84(2):191–215. The founding paper of self-efficacy theory: psychological treatments, whatever their form, are proposed to work by changing a person's expectation that they can perform the needed behaviour. Unread: registered from bibliographic metadata, with no lawful abstract reachable. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Crossref and PubMed, not read. The article is closed access at APA. Unpaywall and OpenAlex call it "green" open access, but their one location is a DOAJ record of an unrelated 2020 Jurnal Psikologi article on thalassemia screening that carries Bandura's DOI by mistake. The copy Stanford hosted with Bandura's papers (web.stanford.edu/dept/psychology/bandura/pajares/Bandura1977PR.pdf) now returns 403 Forbidden. Its archived snapshots are on the Wayback Machine, which this environment's egress policy blocks, and the University of Kentucky mirror of the same collection now redirects away. A PDF of the published article is posted by the Sustainable Sanitation Alliance's library (susana.org), a third party, so it was not read (only its first page was opened, to identify what it was). A human reader with APA access, or one who can open the archived Stanford copy, could promote this. |
| [LIT-546](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-546.md) | The Emotions | Frijda (1986), The Emotions, Cambridge University Press, Studies in Emotion and Social Interaction (ISBN 0-521-30155-6 hardback, 0-521-31600-6 paperback), 544 pp. The canonical statement of Frijda's appraisal and action-readiness theory: emotions are changes in action readiness elicited by appraisal of events as relevant to the individual's concerns, with control precedence over other activity. Unread here; what is said of it comes from the works that cite it. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from bibliographic records, not read. No lawful open copy of the book (544 pages) was found: it has no Crossref DOI, and Open Library lists no open or lendable scan. Under the owner's book rule its reading is replaced by Frijda, Ridderinkhof and Rietveld (2014), [LIT-540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-540.md), read in full, which states the book's central constructs, action readiness, concern and control precedence, in Frijda's words. The closer substitute, Frijda (1988) "The laws of emotion" (American Psychologist 43(5):349–358, DOI 10.1037/0003-066X.43.5.349), was not lawfully reachable from here. A human with library access could read it, or the book, and either would let this entry say more. |
| [LIT-549](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-549.md) | Relational Frame Theory: A Post-Skinnerian Account of Human Language and Cognition | Hayes, Barnes-Holmes & Roche (eds.), Kluwer Academic/Plenum, 2001. The founding book of Relational Frame Theory: human language and cognition are learned, generalized operant behaviour, the arbitrarily applicable relating of events (mutually, in combination, and with transformation of their functions) under contextual control. Eight chapters state the theory, from derived relations to rules and the self; five apply it to development, education, social processes, psychopathology and religion. Unread: registered from Crossref's chapter records, with [LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md) read in its place. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Crossref's book and chapter records, not read; [LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md), a 21-page statement of the same theory by two of its editors, was read in its place. No lawful full text of the book was found. Springer's book page returned a "Client Challenge" bot page, Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy, and Maynooth University's repository (where Barnes-Holmes and Roche deposited many RFT papers) holds no chapter of it. A copy on an Ethiopian national-library server was not used, because it is not an author, institutional or publisher deposit. The editors' own fourteen-page chapter 8, "Relational Frame Theory: A Précis" (pp. 141–154, DOI 10.1007/0-306-47638-x_8), is the part a human reader should take first; a reading of the whole book would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-550](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-550.md) | Emotion and Adaptation | Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation, Oxford University Press, New York (ISBN 0-19-506994-3). The book-length statement of Lazarus's cognitive-motivational-relational appraisal theory; its chapter titles frame emotion through the person–environment relationship, motivation, coping and goal congruence. Eleven chapters run from definition and measurement through motivation and coping, cognition, causality, negative, positive and problematic emotions, development, social influence and health, to research, assessment, treatment and prevention. Unread. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Crossref's chapter records, not read, and no substitute was read either. The book (Oxford University Press, about 560 pages) is closed at the publisher. The shorter work by the same author that states the same theory, Lazarus (1991), "Progress on a cognitive-motivational-relational theory of emotion" (American Psychologist 46(8):819–834, DOI 10.1037/0003-066X.46.8.819), has no lawful open copy. APA does not make it free, and Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar list none. The only full text the web search found is in a bulk upload of Lazarus's journal articles to the Internet Archive by a private user, which is not a lawful source, so I did not open it. Other Lazarus emotion papers (American Psychologist 1991 46(4); Smith & Lazarus 1993; Psychological Inquiry 1995; Journal of Personality 2006) are also closed. His 1993 Annual Review of Psychology chapter is listed as free at the publisher, but annualreviews.org answered with a bot challenge. A human with library access could read the 1991 American Psychologist paper and file it as the read substitute. |
| [LIT-551](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-551.md) | Experiential Avoidance and Behavioral Disorders: A Functional Dimensional Approach to Diagnosis and Treatment | Hayes, Wilson, Gifford, Follette & Strosahl (1996), Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 64(6):1152–1168. Syndromal diagnosis has not found functional pathological processes, and functional analysis has not produced a replicable classification. The paper proposes functional diagnostic dimensions instead, and offers experiential avoidance as one: many disorders are unhealthy efforts to escape and avoid emotions, thoughts, memories and other private experiences. Unread: registered from the abstract. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the PubMed abstract and Crossref, not read. The article is closed access at APA, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy. Copies found online were all third-party postings: a clinician's practice site (actmindfully.com.au), an Argentine ACT group's site (grupoact.com.ar), and a CiteSeerX cache whose source could not be traced because CiteSeerX now redirects to the Wayback Machine, which this environment's egress policy blocks. None is an author, institutional or publisher deposit, so none was used. The ACBS publication page (contextualscience.org) gives the citation and abstract but no file. A human reader with APA PsycArticles access, or the chapter of the same title in The Act in Context (Routledge, 2015, DOI 10.4324/9781315745138-20; Crossref lists it without authors, so that it is a reprint is an inference), could promote this. |
| [LIT-553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-553.md) | Psychological Flexibility as a Fundamental Aspect of Health | Kashdan & Rottenberg (2010), Clinical Psychology Review 30(7):865–878. Psychological health is not a ratio of positive to negative experience or a set of fixed strengths but flexibility: adapting regulation to the situation, balancing time perspectives and life domains, and acting on values while open to experience. Inflexibility marks depression (rumination, emotion context insensitivity) and anxiety (experiential avoidance), and cardiac vagal control is proposed as an integrating marker. Executive functioning, default states and personality underlie it, and dynamic measurement is needed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-436](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-436.md)), in the NIH author manuscript on PubMed Central; worth reading as the review that took "psychological flexibility" out of the ACT literature and made it a general construct of health. Flexibility is adapting to situational demands, reconfiguring mental resources, shifting perspective and balancing competing desires and life domains. Its absence (rumination, emotion context insensitivity, experiential avoidance, low cardiac vagal control) runs through depression and anxiety. Executive functioning, default mental states and personality are its "building blocks". It is a narrative synthesis: no meta-analysis of its own, the causal direction between inflexibility and disorder is left open by its own account, and it asks for dynamic measures in place of the global self-reports the ACT line relies on. |
| [LIT-554](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-554.md) | The Emerging Field of Emotion Regulation: An Integrative Review | Gross (1998), Review of General Psychology 2(3):271–299. Emotions are response tendencies (behavioural, experiential, physiological) called forth by evaluated situations and open to modulation. Emotion regulation is how people influence which emotions they have, when, and how they are experienced and expressed, and it is distinct from coping, mood regulation and defense. A process model places regulation at five points in emotion generation: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change (reappraisal), and response modulation (suppression). The first four are antecedent-focused, the last response-focused. Dysregulation is said to figure in over half of the DSM-IV Axis I disorders and all of Axis II. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-429](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-429.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of the process model of emotion regulation, the five-family scheme (situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change, response modulation) that later regulation research and many therapies are organised around. It defines emotion regulation as "the processes by which individuals influence which emotions they have, when they have them, and how they experience and express these emotions" (p. 275) and separates it from coping, mood regulation and defense. It is a conceptual review: no data of its own, and it says the scheme is "a set of working distinctions" (p. 282). |
| [LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md) | Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: Model, Processes and Outcomes | Hayes, Luoma, Bond, Masuda & Lillis (2006), Behaviour Research and Therapy 44(1):1–25. The ACT model: psychopathology is psychological inflexibility, produced when language (cognitive fusion) and experiential avoidance dominate direct contingencies, and ACT restores flexibility through six processes. A review of correlational, component, mediational and outcome studies finds the model "broadly supportive" but the literature immature, and the evidence suggests ACT works through different processes from traditional CBT. Read in an early author manuscript whose numbers differ from the published paper's. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-431](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-431.md)), but in an early manuscript, not the published text; worth reading as the canonical statement of the ACT model of psychopathology, "psychological inflexibility", and of the six processes ACT targets. Cognitive fusion and experiential avoidance (from [LIT-551](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-551.md)) narrow behaviour, and acceptance, defusion, present-moment contact, self as context, values and committed action restore flexibility. The copy read is an author manuscript in Georgia State University's repository that still carries "xx" placeholders, and its numbers differ from the published paper's as Kashdan and Rottenberg report them (21 studies against 32; an AAQ correlation printed ".030" against ".42"). Use its model and argument, not its numbers. Its own verdict on the evidence is "broadly supportive" but "not mature". |
| [LIT-556](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-556.md) v2 | Reinforcement, Reward, and Intrinsic Motivation: A Meta-Analysis | Cameron & Pierce (1994), Review of Educational Research 64(3):363–423. A hierarchical meta-analysis of about 96 experiments concluding that rewards do not, overall, decrease intrinsic motivation; that verbal rewards increase it; and that the only reliable negative effect is on free-choice time when expected tangible rewards are given for merely doing a task. It called for "abandoning cognitive evaluation theory". Unread: registered from the account of it in [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md) and its authors' restatement in [LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Crossref and from the two papers that analyse it, not read. The article is closed access at SAGE (Review of Educational Research), and Unpaywall finds no open copy. A web search found it only on Scribd, a third-party upload, which was not opened. Its authors' reply to Deci, Koestner and Ryan, Cameron, Banko and Pierce (2001, [LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md)), has since been read and restates this paper's results, but not as a substitute for reading it. A reader with SAGE access could promote this. |
| [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md) v2 | A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation | Deci, Koestner & Ryan (1999), Psychological Bulletin 125(6):627–668. A hierarchical meta-analysis of 128 experiments (101 with free-choice, 84 with self-report measures) on interesting tasks. Tangible rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d = −0.34) and self-reported interest (−0.07); expected rewards did, by every task-related contingency; unexpected and task-noncontingent rewards did not; positive feedback enhanced both measures, but not children's free choice. Read as strong support for cognitive evaluation theory and against Eisenberger and Cameron's behavioural account. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-438](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-438.md)), from an OCR of the scanned published article the authors post on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the largest meta-analysis of the reward-undermining effect and the evidential base SDT cites for it. Across 128 experiments on interesting tasks, expected tangible rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d = −0.36), engagement-, completion- and performance-contingent rewards all did (−0.40, −0.36, −0.28), unexpected and task-noncontingent rewards did not, and positive feedback enhanced it (0.33), though not for children's free choice. It reanalyses Cameron and Pierce ([LIT-556](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-556.md)) study by study. Its categories are CET's, and the rival authors reply, by the abstract of Cameron, Banko and Pierce ([LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md), unread), that the negative effects are circumscribed, not pervasive. |
| [LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md) | The "What" and "Why" of Goal Pursuits: Human Needs and the Self-Determination of Behavior | Deci & Ryan (2000), Psychological Inquiry 11(4):227–268, target article. SDT's case for innate psychological needs, for competence, relatedness and autonomy, defined as nutriments for growth, integrity and well-being and identified functionally, against Hull's drives and Murray's acquired needs. The "why" of a goal (autonomous or controlled regulation) and its "what" (intrinsic or extrinsic aspiration) each predict well-being, because each affects need satisfaction. Thwarted needs yield substitutes, controlled styles and rigid patterns. SDT grounds autonomy in the organism's tendency to self-organize, argued to be an evolved advantage. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-439](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-439.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the published target article on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the full statement of what SDT means by a "need" and why it posits three. Needs are "innate psychological nutriments that are essential for ongoing psychological growth, integrity, and well-being" (p. 228), identified by what follows when they are satisfied or thwarted, not by how strongly people want them. Goals differ in their "why" (autonomous or controlled regulation) and their "what" (intrinsic or extrinsic content), and both matter because of need satisfaction. Thwarting produces need substitutes, controlled regulatory styles and rigid behaviour patterns. It is a target article: the commentaries and the authors' reply in the same issue were not read. |
| [LIT-559](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-559.md) | Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being | Ryan & Deci (2000), American Psychologist 55(1):68–78. Self-determination theory in eleven pages. Three innate psychological needs, for competence, autonomy and relatedness, must be satisfied for growth, integration and well-being; their thwarting is "a principal source of human distress" (p. 74). Motivation differs in kind, not only amount: extrinsic motivation runs from external through introjected and identified to integrated regulation, and becomes more autonomous as a regulation is internalized and integrated with the self. Autonomy is volition, not independence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-442](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-442.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the published article on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the shortest statement of self-determination theory by its authors, and the one most cited. It gives the three basic psychological needs (competence, autonomy, relatedness), the continuum of regulation from amotivation through external, introjected, identified and integrated regulation to intrinsic motivation, and the claim that autonomy is volition, "not ... being independent, detached, or selfish" (p. 74). It is a review: every empirical claim is cited to other papers, nothing is tested here, and it states the reward-undermining result as settled by Deci, Koestner & Ryan ([LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)), which Cameron, Banko & Pierce dispute ([LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md), unread; by its abstract). |
| [LIT-560](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-560.md) | Self-Regulation and the Problem of Human Autonomy: Does Psychology Need Choice, Self-Determination, and Will? | Ryan & Deci (2006), Journal of Personality 74(6):1557–1586. SDT's defence of autonomy as a psychological construct. Philosophers (phenomenologists from Pfänder and Ricoeur; hierarchical accounts from Frankfurt and Dworkin) agree that autonomy is self-endorsement, not independence. On that definition, the critiques fail: behaviourists and Bandura define autonomy as independence from the environment; reductive neuroscience mistakes levels of explanation; nonconscious priming shows autonomy can be compromised, not that it is illusory; too many options is not self-determination; and autonomy matters across cultures. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-441](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-441.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the published article on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the place where SDT states its concept of autonomy against both philosophy and psychology. Autonomy is "regulation by the self", its opposite "heteronomy", regulation "without self-endorsement" (abstract). It is "a matter of degree" (p. 1562), compatible with dependence and with having one option, and lies "not in being independent causes but in exercising their capacity to reflectively endorse or reject prompted actions" (p. 1573). It answers Skinner, Bandura, Pinker, Bargh, Wegner, Schwartz and Iyengar. Its engagement with Frankfurt is thin: two citations of the 1971 paper inside one paragraph on hierarchical accounts, with the analytic detail taken from Dworkin. |
| [LIT-561](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-561.md) | Basic psychological need theory: Advancements, critical themes, and future directions | Vansteenkiste, Ryan & Soenens (2020), Motivation and Emotion 44(1):1–31. Two decades of basic psychological need theory. A basic need must be psychological, essential, inherent, distinct and universal, and its effects pervasive, content-specific, directional and explanatory. Need frustration is not merely low satisfaction: it predicts ill-being, compensatory behaviour and need substitutes, and may be transdiagnostic. Novelty, morality and beneficence are reviewed as candidate fourth needs; none is yet admitted. Universality holds for the effects of need satisfaction, not for how needs are supported. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-440](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-440.md)), from the publisher's typeset PDF that the authors post on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the current statement of basic psychological need theory and of what would make something a basic need. It gives nine criteria (psychological, essential, inherent, distinct, universal; pervasive, content-specific, directional, explanatory), treats need frustration as distinct from low satisfaction and as a candidate transdiagnostic process in psychopathology, and restates universality as "universality without uniformity": the effects of need satisfaction are claimed invariant, the ways needs are supported are not. It is an editorial introduction to two special issues, by SDT's authors, and reviews selectively. |
| [LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md) v2 | Pervasive negative effects of rewards on intrinsic motivation: The myth continues | Cameron, Banko & Pierce (2001), The Behavior Analyst 24(1):1–44. The authors of the 1994 rival meta-analysis re-analyse 145 studies, adopt Deci, Koestner and Ryan's split by initial interest, and code reward contingencies by procedure rather than by cognitive evaluation theory. Rewards for merely doing an interesting task undermine free choice (−0.35, K = 57), as in Deci et al. Rewards for surpassing a score do not, and rewards for beating others enhance. Every effect either way is small. | Active — read in full 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-587](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-587.md)), on the owner's instruction, from the article as hosted by the Cambridge Center for Behavioral Studies; the same article is free in PubMed Central (PMC2731358). Worth reading as the strongest case against pervasive reward undermining, by the authors of the rival meta-analysis, and as the paper that shows the coding scheme decides the result. Re-coding 145 studies by procedure, it finds no overall effect on free choice and enhancement on low-interest tasks. On interesting tasks it finds undermining only for expected tangible rewards loosely tied to performance or earned at less than the maximum, and neutral or positive effects for rewards tied to a score or to beating others. The core effect agrees with Deci et al.; the per-contingency sizes are in figures with no text layer. |

Per its abstract, narrative identity is "a person's internalized and evolving life story, integrating the reconstructed past and imagined future to provide life with some degree of unity and purpose". Unread: registered from the abstract; the construct is read in [LIT-595](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-595.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the Crossref record and its abstract, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. Unread. The book-length statement of picoeconomics: hyperbolic discounting makes a person a population of bargaining interests, and will is the recursive bundling of choices into precedents. | [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), the précis of Breakdown of Will (2001). People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Willpower is the bundling of future choices by treating the present one as a precedent: an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma, not an organ or a top-down ego. The same recursion predicts the will's costs: legalism, circumscribed "lapse districts", motivated blindness to lapses, and rules that favour countable goals over subtle ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), as the substitute for the 2001 book ([LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md)), which the owner suggested and which the précis follows chapter by chapter. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". The same mechanism predicts the will's side effects: legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control. |
| [LIT-589](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-589.md) | Goal Striving, Need Satisfaction, and Longitudinal Well-Being: The Self-Concordance Model | Sheldon & Elliot (1999), JPSP 76(3):482–497. A goal is self-concordant when pursued for identified or intrinsic rather than external or introjected reasons. In three semester-long studies of students, self-concordance predicted sustained effort, which fully mediated its link to attainment; attainment raised well-being more when goals were self-concordant; and accumulated daily experiences of autonomy, competence and relatedness partly mediated attainment's effect on well-being. Paths survived controls for self-efficacy, implementation intentions, avoidance framing and life skills. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-448](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-448.md)); worth reading as the canonical statement of the self-concordance model and its evidence. Goals pursued for identified or intrinsic reasons get more sustained effort, so are better attained (effort fully mediates, in Studies 1 and 3), and attaining them raises well-being more, partly through accumulated daily experiences of autonomy, competence and relatedness. The evidence is three semester-long correlational studies of students (N = 169, 152, 73), with structural models refitted after modification indices, and self-concordance is a self-report of reasons that cannot separate integration from identification. |

Narrative identity is "the internalized and evolving story a person invents to explain how he or she has become the person he or she is becoming", giving a life "unity, moral purpose, and temporal coherence". Agentic and redemptive stories go with well-being and generativity, and cultures supply master narratives. "Biology guides and culture fills in the details." | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-470](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-470.md)), as the read substitute for McAdams & McLean, "Narrative Identity" (2013; [LIT-572](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-572.md)), which has no lawful copy and whose definition this essay takes over word for word.
