| [LIT-602](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-602.md) | The Intimate Contest for Self-Command | Schelling (1980), The Public Interest, Summer 1980, pp. 94-118. People behave sometimes "as if they had two selves" in "continual contest for control", and the tactics of self-management (removing the option, bright lines, monitoring, delays, raising the stakes) are the tactics of managing someone else. A single-dimension model of impatience fits poorly. Which self is authentic is left open. Failures of consumer self-management may be worth "on the order of a trillion dollars". | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-452](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-452.md)), in place of the 1984 Ely Lecture ([LIT-573](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-573.md)), which has no lawful free copy. Worth reading as Schelling's own first statement of "egonomics": a person sometimes behaves "as if they had two selves" that alternate in command, and the tactics people use on themselves (mittens, alarm clocks across the room, bright lines, Christmas savings, deadlines, delays) are the tactics they use to manage another person. It refuses to say which self is authentic in general, and it gives an order-of-magnitude estimate that failures of consumer self-management cost as much as all other consumer-ignorance problems together. |

| [LIT-696](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-696.md) | Towards a Theory of Collective Emotions | von Scheve & Ismer (2013), Emotion Review 5(4):406–413. Collective emotion is synchronous convergence in affective responding towards an event or object. Mutual awareness (contagion, sharing) and group membership (identity, collective intention, norms, collective memory, sentiments) amplify it and can turn "I-mode" into "We-mode" collective emotion. Introduces emotional aperture, the ability to recognise the composition of diverse emotions in a collective such as a group or business unit, and argues that a leader's ability to respond to the patterns of shared emotion that arise in strategic change depends on it. | [LIT-700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-700.md) | Three kinds of collective attitudes | List (2014), Erkenntnis 79(S9):1601–1622. Collective attitudes come in three kinds. Aggregate attitudes summarise members' attitudes by a rule or a market, supervene proposition-wise and need not be rational. Common attitudes are held by all members with common awareness, matter for coordination, and inherit consistency from their unanimity. Corporate attitudes belong to a group agent, guide its action, supervene holistically on members' contributions and must be rational. The kinds are almost logically independent, and fears and hopes divide the same way as beliefs and desires. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-554.md)); worth reading as the disambiguation the collective-attitudes literature needs: aggregate attitudes (summaries, supervening proposition by proposition), common attitudes (unanimous and commonly known, supervening on a slightly enriched base) and corporate attitudes (a group agent's, supervening holistically and not straightforwardly reducible). The three are almost logically independent. A review by its own description, with no new theorem; its value for this record is that it names fears and hopes among the attitudes the split applies to, which gives the collective-emotion debate a vocabulary. |

Organisations treat emotion as the antithesis of rationality, and so regulate it through four institutionalised mechanisms: neutralizing, buffering, prescribing and normalizing emotion. Against this, emotionality and rationality are "interpenetrated", emotion is an inseparable part of organisational life and often functional for the organisation, as shown for motivation, leadership and group dynamics. Unread: from the abstract. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-04 from bibliographic records and the publisher's abstract, not read. No lawful full text was reachable. Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar list no open copy. A web search found only ResearchGate (not used) and a 2014 Arizona State syllabus that lists the paper but does not carry it. | [LIT-705](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-705.md) | Group Agency and Supervenience | List & Pettit (2006), Southern Journal of Philosophy 44(S1):85–105. A group agent's rationality must supervene on its members' contributions, but not proposition by proposition. Three impossibility results show that robust group rationality (complete, consistent, deductively closed group judgments for every profile of rational member judgments) is inconsistent with majoritarian, uniform proposition-wise and proposition-wise supervenience. Premise-based and distributed premise-based procedures show it is consistent with set-wise supervenience, with group judgments that can be discontinuous with the members' judgments on the same proposition. Emergent agency without any member's conception of the group is set aside as unintelligible. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-550.md)); worth reading as the short, formal core of List and Pettit's group agency: a group can be a robustly rational judge only if its judgment on a proposition is not, in general, a function of its members' judgments on that proposition. Group judgments supervene on members' judgments set-wise, not proposition-wise, so a group agent is individualistically unmysterious and still "not directly continuous" with its members. | [LIT-706](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-706.md) | The Ripple Effect: Emotional Contagion and its Influence on Group Behavior | Barsade (2002), Administrative Science Quarterly 47(4):644–675. Two studies of mood contagion in a leaderless group negotiation. In Study 1 (94 undergraduates, 29 groups) a trained confederate showed pleasant or unpleasant, high- or low-energy mood. Members' mood moved with the confederate's valence, by self-report and by blind video-coders, and pleasant contagion predicted more cooperation, less conflict and higher self-rated performance. Study 2 (113 MBA students, 26 groups, no confederate) found mood convergence (ICC .00 to .24) with the same process correlates. Members recognised that others influenced how pleasant they felt, but not that their mood shaped their judged effectiveness. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-551](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-551.md)), from the August 2001 revise-and-resubmit manuscript Wharton deposited in Penn's repository, not the published version; worth reading as the first causal test of emotional contagion in groups. A trained confederate's pleasant or unpleasant mood spread to the members of 29 work groups (self-report and blind video-coders agree), and the more pleasant mood spread, the more cooperative and the less conflicted the group (coder-rated) and the better members rated their own performance. A second study without a confederate found members' moods converging (ICC .00 before, .24 after). Members related their pleasantness to others' conduct but showed no awareness of their mood's bearing on how effective they judged themselves (manuscript p. 37). Valence and energy hypotheses failed or came out mixed. |

Exploration's returns are less certain, more remote and more distant than exploitation's, so adaptive processes refine exploitation faster and become self-destructive in the long run. Behaviour within a work space moves under an effort gradient and a cost gradient toward the boundary of acceptable performance. In defence-in-depth systems, defences degrade unobserved under cost pressure. Accidents arise from many locally reasonable decisions. Improvement means making boundaries visible, not fighting errors. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-584](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-584.md)): the argument in full, the review of research paradigms skimmed, from the author's manuscript in DTU's repository. Worth reading for the model of drift. Under a cost gradient from management and an effort gradient from workers, activity migrates toward the boundary of acceptable performance. In defence-in-depth systems one actor's breach of a defence has no visible effect, so defences erode unobserved. Single-loop learning corrects errors without changing governing values; double-loop learning changes them. Most people espouse double-loop learning but act on Model I: unilateral control, winning, suppressing negative feelings, appearing rational. That produces self-sealing defensive routines in individuals and organizations. A workshop case shows CEOs reproducing the pattern they diagnose. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-561](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-561.md)): in full, from a Word file of the published issue posted by Action Design, a practice founded by Argyris's co-authors. The owner chose to use it, since whether they may post it could not be confirmed. Worth reading as Argyris's compact late statement of the theory of action. Single-loop learning corrects errors within governing values; double-loop learning changes the values. The prevalent theory-in-use, Model I, keeps reasoning tacit and produces organizational defensive routines that are self-sealing. The empirical base is his own workshop transcripts, and the quasi-experimental design is proposed, not run. |

A retrospective on the Viable System Model. Any system able to keep its identity independently in a shared environment has five necessary and sufficient subsystems, and every viable system contains and is contained in one. The model is offered as a scientific model reached by homomorphic mapping, not an analogy. Breakdowns trace to a failing subsystem, as when Three and Five collapse without Four. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-577](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-577.md)): in full except one page, from the 1989 book reprint posted by the Cwarel Isaf Institute, which Beer co-founded. Worth reading as Beer's own retrospective on the Viable System Model. Five subsystems are claimed necessary and sufficient for any system to keep its identity independently, and the structure recurs, since every viable system contains and is contained in one. Breakdowns are diagnosed as failures of a subsystem: without System Four, Systems Three and Five collapse into each other and the system can only react. Limits: the paper declines to expound or validate the model, the copy lacks the page with the synopsis of the subsystems and its figures, and the applications are recalled, not documented. |

Stance as one act with three sides: a speaker evaluates an object, thereby positions themselves, and thereby aligns with other speakers, as three aspects of one dialogic act. Read in full. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-590](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-590.md)), in full, from the author's posted scan of the published chapter; worth reading as the unifying model of stance in conversation: evaluation, positioning and alignment are not kinds of stance but three aspects of one act ("I evaluate something, and thereby position myself, and thereby align with you"), structured as two subjects and a shared object joined by directed vectors. Stance belongs to utterances in dialogic context, takes an object even when none is spoken, and a resonant stance follow must mark itself with too or either. Across all 66 Pew surveys from 2001–2011 that varied the order of two questions, order effects are significant (p = 0.0004) and the q values are not (p = 0.4625); paired context effects across 72 studies correlate at r = −0.82 along the predicted line of slope −1. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-604](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-604.md)); worth reading as the large-scale test of the QQ equality: across 66 Pew surveys chosen without regard to their results, question order changes the answers significantly (p = 0.0004 for the distribution of order-effect χ² values), while the probability of answering the two questions alike stays the same (p = 0.4625 for the q values). Read with the caveats that the supporting information, which holds the proof, the per-study table and the χ² tests, was not reachable and was not read, and that the paper's title claims more than its evidence: the equality is a symmetry constraint that the authors concede a classical model could be built to satisfy, and [LIT-264](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-264.md) shows that data satisfying it are noncontextual. |

Proposes DEVS modelling and simulation (in DEVSimPy) to generate Lévi-Strauss's myth transformations and to map a myth's mythemes onto a landscape, and a "neo-structural" extension of the canonical formula to identity politics. Implemented: myths as mytheme lists, variants generated by user-specified operations, and a Google Earth display of one Corsican folktale. A software demonstration; no structural hypothesis is tested. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-609](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-609.md)), in full, from the publisher's PDF deposited in HAL; worth reading as a statement of a programme rather than a result: the authors propose discrete-event system specification (DEVS) modelling, in their Python environment DEVSimPy, to generate and visualise Lévi-Strauss's transformations of myth, and to extend the canonical formula to identity politics. What the paper implements is modest: a myth is entered as a list of mythemes (term and function), a new variant is produced from a reference myth (Lévi-Strauss's M1 Bororo) by transformation operations stored as an attribute of a model, i.e. specified by the user, and the variants are drawn as a graph; the "validation" plots the 20 mythemes of one Corsican folktale, U Lurcu, on Google Earth in narrative order. No hypothesis about how myths transform is tested. The transformation engine is summarised from the authors' 2020 Symmetry paper, not presented here. |
| [LIT-807](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-807.md) | A Discrete-Event Simulation of Claude Lévi-Strauss’ Structural Analysis of Myths Based on Symmetry and Double Twist Transformations | Santucci, Doja & Capocchi (2020), Symmetry 12(10):1706. Specifies the authors' DEVS models (in DEVSimPy) for generating variants of a myth from a reference myth by Lévi-Strauss's transformations, and a NetworkX graph of the variants produced. Every basic transformation is a user-specified substitution of one term for another across the mythemes; the canonical formula is described but its computation is not; validation is reproduction of 70 Mythologiques myths and 28 Corsican tales by transformations chosen to produce them. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-632](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-632.md)), in full, from the publisher's version deposited in HAL; worth reading as the place where the authors' "transformation model" of Lévi-Strauss is actually specified, and for what that specification turns out to be. A myth is a list of mythemes, each a pair (term a, function x); homology, inversion, opposition and symmetry are all one operation, replacing a term by another term in every mytheme, the inverse, opposite or "symmetric" term being supplied by the user; adding and removing a mytheme complete the set. The canonical formula is explained by Lévi-Strauss's Jealous Potter example and listed as selectable, but no rule for computing it on a mytheme list is given. The "validation" generates 70 myths of the Mythologiques and 28 Corsican folktales by choosing, each time, the transformations that produce them, and reports them correct against Lévi-Strauss's books and Corsican specialists, with no measure. It encodes an analyst's transformations; it does not find or test them. |
| [LIT-822](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-822.md) | Transformation transformed | Descola (2016), HAU 6(3):33–44. A keynote on structuralism as method: meaning lies in contrasts within a set of variants, and a structure is the set of invariant relations that orders transformations between them. Lévi-Strauss used transformation in two regimes, Goethean development of an initial form (kinship) and Thompsonian deformation between given forms (myth, where the analyst chooses the cuts). Descola's fourfold ontology is a Goethean group; structural comparison is anthropology's fairest symmetrization. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-641](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-641.md)), in full, from the PDF on the journal's own site (haujournal.org); worth reading as a short statement, by Lévi-Strauss's student, of what structural analysis is when separated from Lévi-Strauss's philosophy: no phenomenon has meaning in itself, only in contrast with others of its kind, and a structure, unlike a system, is the set of invariant relations that lets one move from one variant to another by transformation. Descola distinguishes two regimes of transformation in Lévi-Strauss: a Goethean one, the development of an initial form into its possible variants (kinship in Les structures élémentaires, and Descola's own four ontologies), and a Thompsonian one, continuous deformation between given forms (myth). In myth, he notes, the group of transformations is a virtual continuum on which the analyst makes the cuts, so the path between variants is the analyst's choice. A keynote lecture; argued, not demonstrated. |
| [LIT-825](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-825.md) | Larger communities create more systematic languages | Raviv, Meyer & Lev-Ari (2019), Proc. R. Soc. B 286:20191262. In a laboratory group-communication game, groups of eight built more systematic (compositional) languages than groups of four, faster and more consistently, with the same total interaction; small groups varied more, as drift would predict. Input variability, greater in larger groups, predicted gains in structure. Group size was isolated from network structure and second-language learners, the confounds of cross-linguistic correlations. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-628](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-628.md)), the main text in full from the publisher's version in the Radboud University repository; the electronic supplementary material was not read. Worth reading as the experiment that isolates community size: 12 groups of four and 12 groups of eight Dutch adults, fully connected, invented a typed language to describe moving shapes over 16 rounds with the same total amount of interaction. Larger groups' languages became more systematic (string distance tracking meaning distance), faster, and ended more systematic; larger groups also varied far less from one another, while some small groups never built structure. Larger groups faced more input variability, and input variability predicted the next round's gain in structure better than shared history did. Communicative success and convergence ended equal. It is a group-interaction paradigm, not a transmission chain: no generation turnover. Source of [THEORY-164](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-164.md). |
| [LIT-828](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-828.md) | Морфология сказки | Propp (1928), Leningrad, Academia (Morphology of the Folktale, English 1958, 2nd ed. 1968). In a hundred Russian wondertales the constants are the characters' functions, defined by their place in the action, not the characters or motifs: 31 functions, always in one order, distributed over seven spheres of action, so all wondertales are of one type and differ in what they omit, how functions are realised and who performs them. Classification by plot is impossible; the wondertale may be morphologically a myth. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-615](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-615.md)), in Russian, the preface and all nine chapters of the 1928 first edition from a library scan in full view at the Internet Archive; the appendices skimmed. Worth reading as the founding structural analysis of narrative: in the wondertales of Afanasyev's collection (nos. 50–151), what stays constant is not the characters or motifs but the functions of the characters, actions defined by their consequence for the plot; there are only 31, they follow one order, and so all wondertales are of one type, differing in which functions they omit, how each is realised and who performs it. Functions fall to seven spheres of action (villain, donor, helper, princess and her father, dispatcher, hero, false hero). Propp holds that a tale can be generated from the scheme, that plot and variant cannot be told apart, and that wondertales in their morphological basis are myth. Source of [THEORY-167](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-167.md). |

Svatava Pirkova-Jakobson, Indiana University Research Center in Anthropology, Folklore and Linguistics, Publication 10 (IJAL 24(4), pt. 3); 2nd ed., revised and edited by Louis A. Wagner, introduction by Alan Dundes, University of Texas Press, 1968. The English translation of Морфология сказки (1928), held as [LIT-828](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-828.md) and read there in Russian. Skimmed in the 1968 edition (chs. II–III and Dundes's introduction): the four theses and 31 functions match the Russian reading; the genre and character terms shift ("folktale", "fairy tale", "dramatis personae"); and Wagner's notes correct Propp's tale references and renumber the tales. | Active — skimmed 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-642](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-642.md)) in the 1968 edition: Dundes's introduction and chs. II–III (pp. 19–65), from copies on University at Buffalo and MIT web pages; the 1958 edition was not seen. Worth reading as the text through which most readers outside Russia met Propp. Chs. II–III carry the four theses and all 31 functions with their definitions and signs, matching the record's reading of the Russian ([NOTE-615](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-615.md)), but with Latin and Greek signs that differ from the Cyrillic. It names the class "fairy tales" under a title its own introducer calls misleading, and alternates "dramatis personae" with "characters". Wagner's 41 notes in those two chapters correct Propp's tale citations and renumber the tales to the later Afanas'ev numbering. The seven roles (ch. VI) were not read. |
| [LIT-834](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-834.md) | A Quantum Question Order Model Supported by Empirical Tests of an A Priori and Precise Prediction | Wang & Busemeyer (2013), Topics in Cognitive Science 5(4):689–710. Models answering an attitude question as projecting a belief state onto the answer's subspace and replacing the state by the normalised projection. Non-commuting projectors are then necessary for order effects, and a parameter-free constraint follows for any state and any projectors: the probability of answering the two questions differently is the same in both orders (the QQ equality). Five of six data sets meet it; the sixth, where background information was read out between the questions, fails it, as predicted. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-636](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-636.md)); worth reading as the source of the quantum question (QQ) model and its QQ equality: if each answer is a Lüders projection of one belief state, the probability of giving different answers to two questions is the same in both orders, whatever the state, the projectors or the dimension. Six data sets bear it out, and the Rose–Jackson poll fails it, as the authors predicted, because new information was inserted between the questions. Read with the caveat that the case against classical rivals is thin: the Bayesian argument is informal and the Markov proof is "available upon request", so the paper shows that unconstrained classical models need not satisfy the equality, not that none can. |
| [LIT-837](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-837.md) v2 | Structuralism | Piaget (1970), Structuralism, trans. and ed. Chaninah Maschler, Basic Books (London: Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1971; reissued 2015). The English edition of Le structuralisme (1968), held as [LIT-802](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-802.md). Skimmed thinly from a publisher's preview (17 pages of chs. I–IV): a structure is a whole under laws of composition, a system of transformations and self-regulating. Logico-mathematical structures are fully reversible (groups); linguistic and social ones are regulated in time but not fully reversible; and a structure is real only if governed from within. | Active — skimmed 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-618](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-618.md)), thinly: the publisher's Google Books preview of the 2015 reissue served only 17 pages of text, pp. 3–63 at one page in four and p. 69, all in chs. I–IV, and none of the chapters on linguistics, the social sciences or philosophy, nor the conclusion. Worth reading as Piaget's definition of structure by wholeness, transformation and self-regulation, and for his distinction between logico-mathematical structures, whose operations all have inverses (groups), and linguistic, social and psychological structures, whose transformations unfold in time under regulations that are "not entirely reversible". He argues that a structure must be "governed from within" to be real, and defines the subject as "the center of functional activity". Read it with the caveat that the skim saw the argument in fragments. |
| [LIT-848](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-848.md) | Large AI models are cultural and social technologies | Farrell, Gopnik, Shalizi & Evans (2025), Science 387(6739):1153–1156, Policy Forum. Large models are best understood not as intelligent agents but as a new cultural and social technology: like writing, print and search they give access to what other people have produced, and like markets, bureaucracies and elections they make lossy, uninvertible summaries of it that can be operated on at scale. The questions that follow are the old ones about such technologies: homogenization or diversity, who gains and who loses, and which countervailing institutions emerge. Argued by historical analogy, without data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-649.md)) from the authors' accepted version (Science galley of 25 February 2025, posted on Farrell's site); worth reading as the compact statement of the view that large models are not agents but a new cultural and social technology, of a kind with writing, print, markets, bureaucracies and elections: lossy summaries of what other humans have produced that let people reorganize it at scale. It is a four-page Policy Forum argued by analogy, with no data. Its one mechanism with consequences is that models fit their training distribution on average, so are least accurate where the data are rare, which may homogenize culture; it sets this against the possibility of "society-like" ecologies of models that keep diversity. |
